Let’s dive into Chapter 3: The 3-6-5 Approach—Building Daily Money Habits.
Now, we’ve talked about the three pillars of money management, but the real magic? It happens when these ideas turn into daily habits you actually live by. That’s where the 3-6-5 approach comes in.
Picture this: just like brushing your teeth or making your bed, managing money can become second nature. The name “3-6-5” is a gentle nudge—reminding us there are 365 days in a year, and every single day is a fresh chance to make smart choices with money.
Here’s the thing: It’s not about making huge changes overnight. Instead, it’s about weaving little actions into your daily routine. Drop a coin in the giving jar. Set aside a bit for savings. Make a thoughtful spending decision. Simple, right? But when you do these things day after day, they start to add up—and that’s when real change happens.
So, how can you make the 3-6-5 approach work in real life? Let’s break it down:
First, try a daily check-in. Just take a minute each day to look at your three jars. Is there money to add? Are there choices to make—maybe about giving, saving, or spending?
Next, set small goals. Maybe the giving jar goes to a local charity, the saving jar helps you work toward a new toy or a family outing, and the spending jar is for treats or activities you love.
And don’t forget to celebrate progress. Hitting a savings goal or donating to a cause you care about—those are wins, and they deserve a little recognition.
What’s especially cool about this approach is how it works for everyone—especially kids, who really thrive on routine and visible progress. When money habits become part of your daily rhythm, they’re as natural as anything else you do around the house. And along the way, you’re reinforcing really important values: generosity, patience, and thoughtful choices.
For families, these daily check-ins aren’t just about money. They’re a chance to connect, to talk about what’s working, and to encourage each other. If questions or challenges pop up, you can tackle them together—before they turn into bigger issues.
And remember, the 3-6-5 approach is super flexible. For younger kids, it might mean sorting coins or picking a cause to support. For older kids—or even adults—you might dig into bigger decisions, like budgeting for something special or planning for the future.
The beauty of this approach is its simplicity. When you break money management down into small, daily steps, it’s way less intimidating—and a whole lot more doable. Plus, every little action you take builds confidence and a sense of control. That’s huge, especially for kids just starting to learn about money.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the 3-6-5 approach turns the big ideas of giving, saving, and spending into real, everyday habits. By making these part of your daily routine, you’re building a strong foundation for financial well-being—one day at a time.
